newsitem.title: USA: US rail intermodal up, carloads off in wk-AAR.
newsitem.headline: US rail intermodal up, carloads off in wk-AAR.

text.p: U.S. rail freight traffic as measured in intermodal volume rose in the week ended September 7 from the same week in 1996, while carloads and ton-miles fell, a railroad group said Thursday in a statement.
The Association of American Railroads reported 140,992 trailers and containers in the week, up 4.6 percent from 134,855 in the year-ago week.
But AAR said carloads fell two percent to 323,757 from 330,416 a year ago, and ton-miles dropped 1.6 percent to 24.0 billion from 24.4 billion.
A ton-mile equals one ton of freight hauled one mile.

"The continued slump in grain traffic is the main story this week," AAR chief economist Harvey Levine said. Grain carloads totaled 16,830 in the week, a 35.6 percent plunge from 26,150 last year. But AAR said carloads of nonmetallic minerals rose 14.3 percent to 10,186 versus 8,914 in the year-ago week. Metals and products also rose 8.8 percent to 11,447 carloads in the week from 10,518 in the same 1996 week.

Lumber and wood products rose 3.6 percent to 4,486 carloads in the week from 4,329 a year ago. Motor vehicles and parts also increased to 17,295 carloads, up three percent from 16,790 in the year-ago week, AAR said.

But metallic ores loadings totaled 18,015, a 12.8 percent drop from 20,656 last year, while primary forest products plunged 17.2 percent to 6,169 carloads from 7,452 a year ago. Loadings of farm products other than grain, crushed stone, grain mill products and coke also posted declines.
In the first 36 weeks of 1996, AAR said ton-miles rose 2.3 percent from the same period last year. Intermodal traffic also rose 0.5 percent, but carloads fell 0.8 percent, AAR said.
AAR also said that the railroad industry's fleet equipment continued to grow in the second quarter of 1996.
It said railroads, private car companies and shippers operated a fleet of 1.23 million freight cars as of June 30, up about 4,000 units from the first quarter and up 1.9 percent from a year earlier.
"Equipment fleets grew in spite of a slowdown in freight car and locomotive installations because deliveries continued to outpace retirements of older equipment," Levine said.
